My group uses a classroom at our college. It's not used after 5 PM, so we're free to do whatever in there.

Up until a year ago, we played in my living room. Then last year, one of our players who'd been out of state for a few years finally moved back home, and has a basement in his house that we converted into a game room.

Here's from when we first built a table for it in preparation for gaming there (this was almost exactly one year ago): http://imgur.com/a/FpPhi

Here's from our very first session using the room: http://imgur.com/a/MMoqu#0

You can see here we've been adding stuff for decorations (art, weapons, etc.): http://imgur.com/a/ZbjmB#0
Two places. One is a gaming club held at a local university. The other is another gaming club, held in a general function hall.

Most sessions I've played was with people from my main circles of friends. We almost always play at one of our houses, basically rotating between the people who have a good gaming space at their place.

I have also participated in a few online sessions, just staying in my room with a microphone and roll20 opened up.

The most unusual place we've played at was on a bus. Most of us were part of our school's marching band, and when we got into DnD, we decided to start a campaign that we'd play on the "band bus" - the school bus that took us to away games every Friday night. It ended up working really well, and once football season was over, we moved the campaign to a traditional tabletop setting and finished it a few months later.

With friends online on Roll20.net. It's surprisingly in depth for a web based application and works really well.

And in my dining room.

My group plays in my half story. One of the group picked up a whiteboard with permanent 1" square lines already on it. We lay that over a folding banquet table. We also use Google Hangouts for our remote player. For short sessions when we are not together at all, we use Roll20.

We used to meet at my flat and have supper together before playing. Then pretty much everyone graduated and moved, so we now play on Skype. I tried using Roll20, but it was enough of a PITA that I just skip it and go into more narrative detail.

I just moved into a new house with a very long narrow room with a fireplace at the end of it. We set a long table there and start a fire, and then I DM with a crackling fire behind me... The mantle and surrounding area is adorned with various horns belonging to the creatures I have slain and mounted, as well as some old barn wood framed drawings on the walls...

Ron Swanson would be very comfortable in our playspace. Haha it sure beats the tiny apartments we have played within in the past. It's nice getting old and finally having an income! (just kidding I have 2 roomates... I will never have nice things.)

I'll try and post a picture later this evening when I get home.
My original plan was to play at a LGS but several of my players want to drink while we play, so we go from house to house a lot.

We play in my dining room off of my kitchen. I've slowly built up the gaming table over time.

First I created an expanding table top over my old table. Then I built a smaller table to use for the game maps over the table. Then I built a dining room table that would seat players better and yet still look nice for guests. And this is the current set up as we use it. I'm sure I will find yet another way to improve it.

To play devils advocate - a trade deal is a deal between countries. Every country wants to get a bit more than they give up. This is impossible to do if everything is public. Each country thinks keeping things secret will benefit their citizens more than the citizens of the other countries.
Democracy is based on the concept of open government. How can the politicians effectively represent their constituents when none of them know what is happening?

Realistically there is no responsibility to announce any detail of a deal while said deal is being negotiated. You may not like that aspect but there's no legal issue at work. After the deal is agreed upon congress gets their shot at it. The fast track status makes things a bit less fungible in that they can only give an up or down vote on the entire package.
